A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, and their main text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 cites supplementary sections absent from its supplied PDF, whereas v3 includes an appendix. This limits judgments about whether some supplementary experiments represent newly introduced coverage.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments on OpenVLA variants, numerical LIBERO results in Tables 1–3, diagnostic experiments and real-robot trials.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulation and real-robot results, with additional supplied evidence on LLaRA transfer, attack sensitivity and failure cases in the appendix.

M1.justification: The UADA optimization objective changes substantively. v1 minimizes the reciprocal of normalized, probability-weighted action discrepancy; v3 explicitly selects the farthest action boundary and minimizes squared error between that target and a normalized soft action (Section 3.2). This changes a central attack loss, while the UPA and TMA approaches remain largely intact.

E1.justification: BridgeData V2, the four LIBERO suites and real-robot manipulation remain. v3 explicitly reports LLaRA evaluation on VIMA difficulty levels L1–L4, but v1 already states that LLaRA transfer results appear in its missing supplement. The supplied material cannot establish whether this represents expanded experimental coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Gaussian random-noise patches as a control in Tables 1–3. Its UMA comparator matches v1's Untarget attack, with a clearer name and explicit cross-entropy objective; it is not an additional comparison method.

E3.justification: v1 states 10 evaluation trials per LIBERO suite; v3 states 50 trials for each of 10 tasks, totaling 500 rollouts per suite. This is a substantial reported evaluation-design revision, although the PDFs do not independently establish which experiments were rerun. The main TMA comparison also stops reporting L1 accuracy, which remains in supplementary analyses.

E4.justification: v3 supplies nonzero TMA target tests, a UPA weight ablation, additional trajectory case studies and a redundant-DoF failure analysis (Tables S2–S3 and Figures S1–S4). Several sensitivity studies were only cross-referenced in the supplied v1. The existing inner-loop, patch-size and four-defense analyses are retained, with revised diagnostic results.

E5.justification: v1's main tables report point estimates; v3 adds failure-rate standard deviations throughout Tables 1–3 and identifies them as variation across tasks within each suite. This substantially expands variability reporting, but does not establish uncertainty across independently seeded training runs.

E6.justification: Main results change extensively: simulation UADA/DoF1 NAD changes from 18.1% to 21.0%, while physical-generation TMA/DoF1 mean LIBERO failure rate changes from 89.1% to 68.7%. Table 3 replaces L1 entries with suite-level failure-rate breakdowns, and supplementary result tables become available. Changed objectives and evaluation settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: The formal UADA definition is revised to introduce a farthest-boundary target and squared-error surrogate. TMA's target domain is also restricted from arbitrary real values to the stated action bounds. These are localized mathematical-definition changes; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: Both versions claim pioneering VLA-specific patch attacks, substantial simulation and physical vulnerabilities, and the need for stronger defenses. The headline 100% simulation and 43% real-world figures remain. v3's abstract explicitly mentions two untargeted objectives, both already present in v1's main text.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation of weaker attacks on task-redundant rotational DoFs, discusses dataset variability as a reason for different NAD values, and proposes camouflage and task-aware targeting as future directions. The broader robot-joint resemblance hypothesis and proposed defense strategies were already present in v1.

D1.justification: v3 supplies exact patch-placement coordinates, untransformed test-patch instructions, timeout and defense settings, and concrete physical tasks with a benign-success selection rule. Most optimizer hyperparameters are relocated rather than changed. Named code and project links replace the anonymous link, but the PyTorch/A100 disclosure and explicit sampling/clipping steps in Algorithm 1 disappear.

R1.justification: v3 adds Kurdila and Ben-Tzvi's robotics text to support the redundant-DoF discussion and removes the Jin reasoning-length and PyTorch references. The human–robot safety review is moved to the appendix, not removed, and the central positioning relative to VLA and adversarial-attack research remains stable.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: safety-related work moves to the appendix, NAD becomes a separate methodology subsection, implementation moves into Experiments, and detailed settings move into supplementary sections. Method and results passages are rewritten, baseline explanations expand, and the author block and acknowledgements change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a radar chart to a composite threat illustration, patch examples and bar chart. Table 3 becomes a full-width comparison with suite-level breakdowns; Tables 1–2 gain controls, averages and variability columns. Main figures are revised or relocated, and Tables S1–S3 and Figures S1–S4 are supplied.

improvement.justification: The stronger stated evaluation protocol, random-noise controls, task-wise variability and supplied sensitivity/failure analyses improve empirical scrutiny. These gains are moderated by losing main-table TMA action-accuracy results and some reproducibility details. Appendix inconsistencies also limit the improvement: Section S2 misattributes several Table S1 scores, and the selected UPA configuration's 93.4% failure rate in Table S3 is not reconciled with Table 1's 89.7%.
